title: 01 — Data Engineering Foundations
html:
01 — Data Engineering Foundations

The one idea: operational systems are built to run the business one record at a time; analytical systems are built to understand the business across millions of records at once. Data engineering is the bridge between the two, and nearly every design decision in the field comes from the tension between those two shapes of workload.

1. What data engineering is

A data engineer builds and runs the systems that take data from where it is created (application databases, event streams, third-party APIs, files dropped by partners) and turn it into datasets that other people and programs can depend on.

"Depend on" is the important part. Anyone can copy a table once. The job is to make that copy:

  • Correct — the numbers match the source, duplicates are handled, late data is accounted for.
  • Repeatable — the pipeline runs every hour or every day without a human babysitting it.
  • Recoverable — when it fails (it will), you can rerun it without corrupting anything.
  • Understandable — people can find the data, know what each column means, and know where it came from.
  • Affordable — compute and storage costs grow sensibly with data volume, not explosively.

If you come from backend engineering, the closest analogy is: a data engineer is a backend engineer whose "users" are analysts, data scientists, dashboards and ML models, and whose "database" is often petabytes of files on object storage.

2. The roles around the data

Titles vary between companies, but the responsibilities cluster like this.

Role Owns Typical tools Main output
Data engineer Ingestion, pipelines, storage layout, reliability, performance Spark, SQL, Python, Kafka, Databricks, Airflow Trusted, timely datasets (bronze/silver, often gold)
Analytics engineer Business logic in SQL, dimensional models, metric definitions, tests SQL, dbt, semantic layers Clean gold models and metrics analysts can use directly
Data analyst Answering business questions, reporting, dashboards SQL, Power BI, Tableau, Excel Insights, reports, dashboards
Data scientist Statistical analysis, experiments, predictive models Python, notebooks, pandas, scikit-learn Models, experiment readouts, forecasts
ML engineer Taking models to production: features, training pipelines, serving, monitoring MLflow, feature stores, model serving, Python Reliable model endpoints and batch scoring jobs
Data platform engineer The platform other data people build on: workspaces, compute policies, CI/CD, security, cost controls Terraform, Databricks admin, cloud IAM, networking A paved road — templates, guardrails, shared services

The boundaries are blurry on purpose. In a small team one person does all of it. In a large organisation the handoffs between these roles are where most data problems start, which is why data contracts and lineage (chapter 10) matter so much.

3. The data lifecycle

---
title: The data lifecycle — generate to govern
---
flowchart LR
    G["Generate<br/>apps, devices, partners"] --> I["Ingest<br/>batch or streaming"]
    I --> S["Store<br/>lake, warehouse, lakehouse"]
    S --> T["Transform<br/>clean, join, model, aggregate"]
    T --> V["Serve<br/>BI, SQL, ML, APIs, reverse ETL"]
    GV["Govern<br/>catalog, access, quality, lineage, retention"] -.-> I
    GV -.-> S
    GV -.-> T
    GV -.-> V
Stage Key questions Common failure modes
Generate Who produces this data? Can they change its shape without telling us? Silent schema changes, missing events, clock skew on devices
Ingest Pull or push? Full copy or incremental? How fresh must it be? Double-loading, missed deletes, API rate limits, partial files
Store Which format? How is it partitioned? How long do we keep it? Millions of tiny files, no retention policy, wrong partition key
Transform Where does business logic live? Is it idempotent? Logic duplicated in five places, non-deterministic reruns
Serve Who reads it and with what latency? Through which interface? Dashboards querying raw tables, no semantic layer, conflicting metrics
Govern Who may see what? Is PII protected? Can we delete a customer? Over-broad access, untracked PII copies, no lineage

Governance is drawn as wrapping the other stages because it is not a step you do at the end; it has to be designed in at every stage.

4. OLTP vs OLAP

This is the single most important distinction in the field.

Aspect OLTP (Online Transaction Processing) OLAP (Online Analytical Processing)
Purpose Run the business: place an order, update a balance Understand the business: revenue by region by month
Typical query Read or write one row by key Scan millions of rows, aggregate a few columns
Query shape SELECT * FROM orders WHERE id = 42 SELECT region, SUM(amount) FROM orders GROUP BY region
Concurrency Thousands of small concurrent transactions Fewer, much larger queries
Schema Normalised (3NF) to avoid update anomalies Denormalised (star schema, wide tables) to avoid joins
Storage layout Row-oriented Column-oriented
Data volume Current state, GB to low TB Full history, TB to PB
Latency target Milliseconds Seconds to minutes
Examples SQL Server, PostgreSQL, MySQL, Cosmos DB Databricks SQL, Snowflake, BigQuery, Synapse, ClickHouse

Why not just run analytics on the OLTP database? Three reasons:

  1. Contention. A 10-minute analytical scan competes with checkout traffic for CPU, memory and locks.
  2. Shape. Row storage reads every column of every row even when you need two columns.
  3. History. OLTP systems keep current state. "What was this customer's address last March?" is usually unanswerable there.

So we copy data out of OLTP systems into an OLAP-friendly store. That copying is most of data engineering.

5. Structured, semi-structured and unstructured data

Type What it looks like Examples How you usually store it
Structured Fixed columns with known types Relational tables, CSV exports with a stable header Tables (Delta, Parquet, warehouse tables)
Semi-structured Self-describing, nested, fields may vary per record JSON events, Avro messages, XML, log lines with key-value pairs Raw as-is in bronze, then parsed into columns (or kept as a VARIANT/STRUCT/MAP column)
Unstructured No inherent schema PDFs, images, audio, free text, emails Files in object storage (e.g. Unity Catalog volumes) plus a metadata table pointing at them

A practical rule: land semi-structured data raw, parse it downstream. If you parse JSON at ingestion and the producer adds a field, you lose it. If you store the raw payload in bronze, you can always re-parse.

6. Schema-on-write vs schema-on-read

Schema-on-write Schema-on-read
When the schema is applied When data is written; bad data is rejected When data is queried; the reader interprets the bytes
Classic home Relational databases, data warehouses Data lakes (files in folders), Hive over raw text
Strength Guarantees: every row matches the declared types Flexibility: land anything now, decide later
Weakness Rigid: upstream changes break loads Every reader must re-interpret, so errors surface late and inconsistently

Modern lakehouse table formats (Delta Lake, Iceberg) sit in the middle: the table has a declared schema that is enforced on write, but the schema can evolve in controlled ways (add a column, widen a type). Bronze layers often behave closer to schema-on-read (keep the raw payload), while silver and gold are strictly schema-on-write.

7. Sources and sinks

A source is anything you read from; a sink is anything you write to. The same system can be both.

Category Sources Typical ingestion method
Relational databases SQL Server, PostgreSQL, Oracle, MySQL JDBC batch extract, or CDC from the transaction log
NoSQL Cosmos DB, MongoDB, DynamoDB Change feed / change streams, export
Event streams Kafka, Azure Event Hubs, Kinesis Streaming consumer
Files CSV/JSON/Parquet drops in blob storage, SFTP File listing or file-arrival notifications (Auto Loader)
SaaS APIs Salesforce, Stripe, Workday REST pulls with pagination and rate limits, or a managed connector
Logs and telemetry App logs, clickstream, IoT Streaming or batched file drops
Category Sinks
Lakehouse tables Delta / Iceberg tables in object storage
Warehouses Databricks SQL, Snowflake, Synapse, BigQuery
Serving stores Low-latency key-value or relational stores for applications
Operational tools CRMs, marketing platforms (via reverse ETL)
Search and vector indexes Elasticsearch, vector search indexes for RAG
Other streams Kafka topics for downstream consumers

8. Batch vs streaming at a glance

Batch Streaming
Data Bounded: "everything that arrived yesterday" Unbounded: events keep arriving forever
Trigger Schedule or upstream completion Continuous, or frequent micro-batches
Latency Minutes to hours Sub-second to minutes
Complexity Lower: rerun the whole day if it fails Higher: state, late data, checkpoints, always-on compute
Cost Pay only while it runs Often pay for always-on compute (unless you use triggered streaming)
Good for Daily reporting, finance close, model training Fraud signals, live operations dashboards, alerting

A key insight from Spark's Structured Streaming: batch is just streaming over a bounded input. The same code can often run either way, and "streaming that runs once and stops" (the availableNow trigger) is a very common production pattern because it gets you incremental processing without always-on cost. Chapter 03 covers the full taxonomy.

9. The modern data stack

"Modern data stack" is a loose label for the cloud-native toolset that became common from about 2016 onwards. Its defining traits:

  • Cloud object storage and elastic compute, separated so each scales independently.
  • ELT instead of ETL: load raw data first, transform inside the warehouse/lakehouse with SQL.
  • Managed ingestion connectors instead of hand-written extract scripts.
  • SQL-first transformation with version control and tests (dbt, declarative pipelines).
  • Orchestration as code (Airflow, Databricks Workflows, Dagster).
  • Open table formats (Delta, Iceberg) so multiple engines can read the same data.
  • A semantic layer and BI on top, and increasingly reverse ETL pushing results back into operational tools.
---
title: Modern data stack — layers and example tools
---
flowchart TB
    L1["Ingestion<br/>CDC tools, managed connectors, Auto Loader, Kafka"]
    L2["Storage<br/>ADLS / S3 / GCS with Delta or Iceberg tables"]
    L3["Compute and transformation<br/>Spark, Databricks SQL, dbt, declarative pipelines"]
    L4["Orchestration<br/>Workflows, Airflow, Data Factory"]
    L5["Semantic and serving<br/>metric definitions, SQL warehouses, feature stores"]
    L6["Consumption<br/>Power BI, notebooks, ML, reverse ETL"]
    L7["Cross-cutting: catalog, lineage, quality, access control, cost monitoring"]
    L1 --> L2 --> L3 --> L5 --> L6
    L4 -.-> L1
    L4 -.-> L3
    L7 -.-> L2
    L7 -.-> L3

The honest caveat: stitching ten best-of-breed tools together creates its own integration and governance burden. Platforms like Databricks pitch themselves as consolidating many of these layers (storage format, compute, orchestration, catalog, BI, ML) in one place. Neither approach is free; the trade-off is flexibility versus integration effort.

10. Mental models worth keeping

  1. Data has gravity. Moving petabytes is slow and expensive; move compute to data, not the other way round.
  2. Storage is cheap, recomputation is not always cheap, and lost raw data is unrecoverable. Keep raw data.
  3. Every pipeline will be rerun. Design so a rerun produces the same result (idempotency).
  4. Every source will change without warning. Detect schema drift; do not assume.
  5. Time is two things. When an event happened (event time) and when you saw it (processing time) differ, and the gap matters.
  6. The consumer defines "correct". A number is only right relative to a definition someone agreed to.

Azure / .NET mapping

Concept Azure / Microsoft equivalent
OLTP source Azure SQL Database, SQL Server, Cosmos DB
Object storage for the lake Azure Data Lake Storage Gen2 (ADLS Gen2)
Streaming ingestion Azure Event Hubs (Kafka-compatible endpoint available)
Batch ingestion and orchestration Azure Data Factory, Fabric Data Factory
Lakehouse compute Azure Databricks, Microsoft Fabric
BI Power BI
Catalog and governance Unity Catalog, Microsoft Purview
Producing events from .NET Azure.Messaging.EventHubs or Confluent.Kafka client libraries

For a .NET engineer: your ASP.NET Core service writing to Azure SQL is the OLTP source. The outbox pattern you may already use for messaging is also a clean way to publish change events for analytics without coupling to the database log.

Review checklist

  • I can explain the difference between OLTP and OLAP and why analytics should not run on the OLTP database.
  • I can name the six stages of the data lifecycle and a failure mode for each.
  • I can distinguish the data engineer, analytics engineer and ML engineer roles.
  • I know why semi-structured data should be landed raw before parsing.
  • I can explain schema-on-write vs schema-on-read and where a lakehouse sits.
  • I can describe when batch is enough and when streaming is justified.
  • I can list the layers of the modern data stack and one tool in each.
